en: The Ritual Manual for the Sadhana of Mahāmāyā by Kukkurīpāda.
Homage to Vajraḍāka!

First, having performed the cleansing of the mouth and other preliminary rites, seated upon a soft cushion, one visualizes the seed-syllable *hūṃ* within a solar disc at one’s own heart. One then contemplates Karuṇācalavajra before oneself, with the colors, arms, and weapons as will be described. Having performed the worship, the confession of sins, the rejoicing in merit, the dedication of merit, the taking of the three refuges, and so forth, up to the making of aspirations, one [contemplates] the syllables of the name within one’s own body, speech, and mind: *he* signifies that all phenomena are devoid of cause;
*ha* signifies that all phenomena have abandoned arising.
"E" signifies that all phenomena are free from seeking;
"Ru" signifies that all phenomena are like an echo;
"Ra" signifies that all phenomena are endowed with delight.
*U* signifies that all phenomena possess the nature of arising and ceasing;
*ka* signifies that all phenomena are endowed with every happiness;
*a* signifies that the letter *a* is the gateway to all phenomena because they are unarisen from the very beginning.
Having thus reflected and meditated upon emptiness, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*.

Having dispelled obstacles with the syllable *huṃ* and visualized the vajra-fence, one beholds the seed-syllable *huṃ* within a sun-maṇḍala at the center of a red four-petaled lotus in the midst of the eight cremation grounds. Then, the four goddesses, whose natures consist of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), urge [the practitioner] on with the glorious Vajra-song in the Inner Sadhana:
O friend, the lotus has blossomed by the sound of the lute;
alas, alas! it has been mounted upon the dance with great joy.
By the sun’s rays, the lotus has blossomed with great joy;
Alalalalaho, with great affection, he has ascended and dances.
"By means of the dance of the Vajraḍākinīs, one should cause Vajrasattva to enter.

Immediately following this song, through the mental realization that all things are bound by illusion, one should visualize Karuṇācalavajra, arisen from the syllable *HŪṂ*. He has four faces—blue, yellow, white, and dark—and four arms;

in his right hands he holds a skull-cup and an arrow, and in his left hands he holds a khaṭvāṅga staff and a bow. He stands in a wrathful posture (*raudrāsana*), possesses three eyes, wears a garland of fresh severed heads, is adorned with a crown of skulls, and is embellished with ornaments of bone.

His face is slightly terrifying with bared fangs, and his tawny hair stands erect. He is marked by the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*): the syllable *cī* is yellow on the body; *oṃ* is white in the two eyes; *huṃ* is red in the two ears; *kha* is white in the nose; *āḥ* is white in the throat; and *re* is red in the heart. Embraced by a consort of his own radiance, he occupies the expanse of space as the consecrated Vajradhara.

Having visualized oneself as the *kīla* empowered by body, speech, and mind, whose intrinsic nature is the wisdom of the utterly pure *dharmadhātu*, thereupon, on the eastern petal, one meditates upon Vajraḍākinī, blue in color, with four faces—blue, yellow, red, and dark green—and four arms; in her left hands she holds a *khaṭvāṅga* and a bell, and in her right hands she holds a vajra and a skull-cup; she is the essence of the earth element and the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).

On the southern petal is Ratnaḍākinī, yellow in color, with four faces—yellow, blue, red, and dark green—and four arms; she holds a banner and a bodice in her left hands, and a trident and a jewel in her right hands, and her nature is the wisdom of the equality of the water element.

On the western petal is Padmaḍākinī, white and reddish in color, with four faces—red, yellow, blue, and dark green—and four arms; she holds a bow and a skull-cup in her left hands, and an arrow and a double-lotus in her right hands, and her nature is the wisdom of discernment of the fire element.

On the northern petal is Viśvaḍākinī, dark green in color, with four faces—dark green, yellow, red, and blue—and four arms. In her left hands she holds a noose and a skull-cup; in her right hands she holds a *khaṭvāṅga* and a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*). Her nature is the performance of the activity of the wind element.

All these goddesses stand in the wrathful posture (*raudrāsana*), their heads adorned with garlands of skulls, wearing necklaces of fresh severed heads, possessing three eyes, their faces slightly terrifying with bared fangs, their tawny hair blazing and standing upright, and they are encircled by a mass of radiating rays.

Having thus meditated upon oneself as Karuṇācalavajra surrounded by the four goddesses, and having visualized, according to the oral instruction, the maṇḍalas of Vāyu, Mahendra, Varuṇa, and Agni at the head, heart, navel, and secret place, the practitioner of mantra should perform the neuter recitation (*napuṃsakajāpa*).

When fatigued, having performed the mantra recitation— *oṃ āḥ hrīṃ huṃ phaṭ*— the yogin, whose nature is the Dharma established in the mantra that is the essence of all phenomena equal to cyclic existence (*bhava*), may perform all activities regarding sense objects and so forth.
"For the sake of liberation according to the Prākṛta-kalpa.
Thus ends the *Mahāmāyāsādhanopāyikā*.
"This is the work of the venerable Kukkuripāda."
